title: AutoSaddler: Automatic Harness Optimization with Durable Updates from Agent Execution Traces
claim: Our method reaches higher accuracy with far fewer executions and optimization traces than competing optimizers, which plateau lower.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots, shared y-axis, step curves with scattered candidate points
description: Two side-by-side line plots share a y-axis, Best Dev Set Accuracy (%), running from about 45 to 75. Panel (a), titled Compute Efficiency, plots accuracy against Total Tasks Executed, 0 to 2,800. Panel (b), titled Learning Efficiency, plots accuracy against Total Traces Leveraged for Optimization. Each panel has three monotone step curves: AutoSaddler in teal, Meta-Harness in red, and GEPA in navy. All three start from one black dot near 47.5%. Faint scatter points in matching colors show individual candidate evaluations. In both panels the teal curve climbs highest, to about 72%. In (a) it gets there at about 1,000 tasks, while the red curve plateaus near 61.5% after about 2,800. In (b) the teal curve rises almost vertically within roughly 150 traces, far to the left of the red curve. Each panel has a legend at lower right.
caption: Comparison of optimization performance and efficiency on GAIA2. (a) \proposed{} reaches 72.3% dev accuracy with ${\sim}$1,000 total task executions, whereas GEPA and Meta-Harness saturate at 64.6% and 61.5%, respectively, despite consuming ${\sim}$\textbf{2{,}800} task executions. (b) When measured by the number of execution rollouts leveraged for optimization, \proposed{} achieves its best performance after consuming only 147 traces, ${\sim}$10$\times$ fewer than Meta-Harness (1,400 traces).
abstract: LLM agents remain unreliable on long-horizon tasks, where small local failures can compound over extended interactions and lead to overall task failure. Although external harnesses can substantially improve robustness, harness design remains a manual and expensive process that requires searching over a large space of prompts, tool configurations, and control logic. We propose AutoSaddler, an automatic harness optimization framework that formulates harness improvement as an offline learning problem and iteratively updates the harness using failure signals from mini-batches. AutoSaddler combines failure-trace diagnosis, structured patch generation that treats the harness as code, and validation-based update selection. Experiments on GAIA2, SWE-Bench Pro, and Terminal-Bench 2.0 show that AutoSaddler substantially improves agent performance over the corresponding base harnesses, achieving gains of 9.0, 9.6, and 10.0 percentage points, respectively. Ablation studies further suggest that effective harness optimization benefits from three ingredients: deep debugging rather than shallow reflection, targeted modifications rather than unconstrained editing, and generalization-aware selection rather than trajectory-specific repair. Together, these results suggest that automatic harness optimization is a promising path toward more performant and reliable agent systems.
